misconceptions.statement: Profit percent is always found by dividing the profit by the selling price.
misconceptions.why: The selling price is the bigger and more visible number in a sale, so it feels like the whole.
misconceptions.fix: Profit and loss percent are found on the cost price, because the cost is what was invested.

probe.question: A shirt bought for Rs 200 is sold for Rs 250. What is the profit percent?

misconceptions.root_belief: the final or biggest quantity is always the whole
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student errors in percentage base identification

misconceptions.statement: If the selling price is more than the cost price you have a loss.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up which of the two numbers is paid and which is received.
misconceptions.fix: Profit happens when SP is greater than CP; loss happens when SP is less than CP.

probe.question: CP is Rs 400 and SP is Rs 460. Is it profit or loss?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Cost price and selling price mean the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Both are called the price of the article in daily talk.
misconceptions.fix: Cost price is what the seller pays to get the article; selling price is what the buyer pays the seller.

probe.question: A trader buys for Rs 80 and sells for Rs 100. What is the cost price?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Repair and transport money spent after buying is not part of the cost price.
misconceptions.why: Students think cost price is only the amount written on the bill of purchase.
misconceptions.fix: Overheads such as repair, transport and labour are added to the purchase price to get the cost price.

probe.question: A cycle is bought for Rs 1000 and Rs 200 is spent on repairs, then sold for Rs 1320. Profit percent?

misconceptions.root_belief: only the first or obvious number counts
misconceptions.source_hint: textbook error analyses in commercial arithmetic

misconceptions.statement: Loss percent can be more than 100 if the loss is large.
misconceptions.why: Gain percent can exceed 100, so students assume loss can too.
misconceptions.fix: Loss cannot exceed the cost price, so loss percent is at most 100.

probe.question: Can a loss percent be 150%?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if the article is sold very cheaply

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule that works one way works the opposite way

misconceptions.statement: A 25% gain means the selling price is 25 more than the cost price whatever the cost is.
misconceptions.why: Students treat percent as a fixed number of rupees.
misconceptions.fix: A 25% gain is one quarter of the cost price, so the rupee gain depends on the cost.

probe.question: An article costs Rs 80. Find the SP for a 25% gain.

misconceptions.root_belief: percent is an absolute amount, not a part
misconceptions.source_hint: research on percent as absolute versus relative quantity

misconceptions.statement: To find the cost price when a 20% profit gives SP, subtract 20% of the SP from the SP.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the percent to the number given in the question.
misconceptions.fix: SP is 120% of CP, so CP is SP divided by 1.2, not SP minus 20% of SP.

probe.question: An article is sold for Rs 600 at a 20% profit. Find the cost price.

misconceptions.root_belief: percent is always taken of the given number

misconceptions.statement: A 20% gain followed by a 20% loss brings you back to the starting price.
misconceptions.why: Students think plus and minus of the same number cancel.
misconceptions.fix: The two percents are on different bases, so the final price is 96% of the start, a 4% net loss.

probe.question: A price Rs 100 rises 20% and then falls 20%. What is the final price?

misconceptions.root_belief: opposite changes of the same size cancel
misconceptions.source_hint: research on percentage increase and decrease reversal

misconceptions.statement: Selling at x% profit and then buying back at x% less gives no overall change.
misconceptions.why: Students pay attention to the equal percent and ignore which price it is taken on.
misconceptions.fix: Every percent is on its own starting price, so equal up and down percents leave a small net loss.

probe.question: Rs 500 is increased by 10% and then decreased by 10%. Find the final amount.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Discount is always a percent of the cost price.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the rule that profit percent uses the cost price.
misconceptions.fix: Discount is taken on the marked price, which is the price written on the article.

probe.question: MP is Rs 500, CP is Rs 400, discount is 10%. What is the discount?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case applies to all cases
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of base confusion in commercial percentages

misconceptions.statement: The discount amount is the new price you pay.
misconceptions.why: The discount is the number in the offer, so students read it as the answer.
misconceptions.fix: Discount is what you save; the price paid is the marked price minus the discount.

probe.question: MP is Rs 800 with 25% discount. What do you pay?

misconceptions.root_belief: the last number computed is the final answer

misconceptions.statement: A discount means the shopkeeper makes a loss.
misconceptions.why: Students link giving money off with losing money.
misconceptions.fix: A discount is taken from the marked price, which is usually above cost, so the seller can still gain.

probe.question: CP is Rs 600, MP is Rs 1000, discount 20%. Is there a loss?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because there is a discount

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Two successive discounts of 20% and 10% equal a single discount of 30%.
misconceptions.why: Students add percents as ordinary numbers.
misconceptions.fix: The second discount is on the reduced price, so the net discount is 28%, less than 30%.

probe.question: A 20% and then 10% discount equal one discount of how much?

misconceptions.root_belief: percents can be added like plain numbers
misconceptions.source_hint: research on additive reasoning with percentages

misconceptions.statement: The second discount is calculated on the original marked price.
misconceptions.why: Students keep using the marked price as the only base they know.
misconceptions.fix: The second discount is on the price after the first discount.

probe.question: MP Rs 1000, discounts 10% and 10%. Final price?

misconceptions.root_belief: the first number given is always the base
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of base shifting in successive percent problems

misconceptions.statement: Changing the order of two successive discounts changes the final price.
misconceptions.why: Students think the first discount does more work than the second.
misconceptions.fix: The final price is the same in either order because it is a product of the same factors.

probe.question: Is 20% then 10% cheaper than 10% then 20% on Rs 1000?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the bigger discount first gives a lower price

misconceptions.root_belief: order always matters in a sequence

misconceptions.statement: GST is included in the price and is subtracted from it.
misconceptions.why: Prices in shops often already include tax, so students think GST reduces the price.
misconceptions.fix: GST is added to the price before tax, so the bill is higher than the base price.

probe.question: An item costs Rs 500 and GST is 18%. What is the bill?

misconceptions.root_belief: tax or fee is a reduction

misconceptions.statement: To remove 18% GST from a bill of Rs 1180, subtract 18% of 1180.
misconceptions.why: Students use the percent on the number given.
misconceptions.fix: The bill is 118% of the base price, so divide by 1.18 to get Rs 1000.

probe.question: A bill of Rs 1180 includes 18% GST. Find the price before GST.

misconceptions.root_belief: percent is always taken of the given number

misconceptions.statement: GST is charged on the marked price, not on the price after discount.
misconceptions.why: Students use the marked price as the base for everything.
misconceptions.fix: GST is charged on the price the buyer actually pays after discount, the taxable value.

probe.question: MP Rs 1000, discount 10%, GST 5%. Find the bill.

misconceptions.root_belief: the first number given is always the base

misconceptions.statement: CGST and SGST are each equal to the full GST rate.
misconceptions.why: Students see 9% and 9% and do not connect them to the 18% total.
misconceptions.fix: GST is split equally between CGST and SGST, so each is half the rate, and together they make the full GST.

probe.question: GST is 12%. What are CGST and SGST?

misconceptions.root_belief: parts of a whole each equal the whole

misconceptions.statement: Markup percent and profit margin percent on an item are the same number.
misconceptions.why: Both describe the extra over cost and are used loosely together.
misconceptions.fix: Markup is found on the cost price and margin on the selling price, so for the same profit the markup is larger.

probe.question: CP Rs 80, SP Rs 100. What are markup and margin?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: business mathematics education studies on base confusion

misconceptions.statement: A marked price is the cost price plus the discount.
misconceptions.why: Students link the tag price to the discount word only.
misconceptions.fix: The marked price is the tag price chosen by the seller; the discount is subtracted from it to get the sale price.

probe.question: MP is Rs 600 with 10% discount. Cost price is Rs 500. What is the sale price?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: A profit of Rs 20 always means 20 percent profit.
misconceptions.why: The same number is read as both rupees and percent.
misconceptions.fix: Percent profit depends on the cost price, so Rs 20 is 20% only when the cost is Rs 100.

probe.question: A toy is bought for Rs 50 and sold for Rs 70. What is the profit percent?

misconceptions.root_belief: percent is an absolute amount, not a part
misconceptions.source_hint: research on percent versus absolute amount confusion

misconceptions.statement: A larger percent gain always means a larger rupee gain.
misconceptions.why: Students compare percents without checking the cost price.
misconceptions.fix: The rupee gain is percent times cost, so a small percent of a large cost can be bigger than a large percent of a small cost.

probe.question: Which is more profit: 30% on Rs 100 or 10% on Rs 1000?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: research on proportional reasoning with percents
